source_text:
Ποιμὴν ἀν αὐχμῷ καὶ καύσωνι, ὄμβρῳ καὶ χιόνι καὶ πάχνῃ συζῶν, καλύβην ἔχων τὰς ἐξοχὰς τῶν πετρῶν, τροφὴν τυρὸν καὶ γάλα, ἱμάτιον ἀνέργαστον τῶν προβάτων τὴν δοράν, ἀλλ' οὗτος ὁ
ἄγροικος, ὁ πένης, ὁ ὄρεσιν προσομιλῶν Ζακχαίῳ περιέπιπτεν δεκατευόμε νος τὰ θρέμματα, ἐννόμως λῃστευόμενος, ἄνευ ξίφους ἀναιρού μενος. Σιδήρῳ γὰρ ὁ πληγεὶς καὶ ῥεῖον τὸ τραῦμα λαβὼν οἴχεται ἀναισθησίᾳ φυγὼν τοῦ πάθους τὴν χαλεπότητα, ὁ δὲ ἀκουσίῳ πενίᾳ τετοξευμένος θάνατον ἔχει τὸν πόνον καὶ τέθνηκεν· οὐχ ἅπαξ δαπανούμενος, θνῄσκει δὲ ἀεὶ κατὰ μικρόν. Καὶ ἵνα συντόμως εἴπω, ὥσπερ στρατιώταις τὰ δυσάλωτα φρούρια καὶ τοῖς κυβερνήταις αἱ ὕφαλοι πέτραι καὶ τοῖς πολεμοῦσιν οἱ ὕποπτοι λόχοι, οὕτως ἐμπόροις καὶ ὁδοιπόροις, βουκόλοις καὶ ποιμέσιν Ζακχαῖος φευκτὸς ἦν.Ἀλλ' οὗτος οὕτω περὶ τὴν ἄλογον τῶν χρημάτων συλλογὴν μεμηνὼς ζητῶν τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἰδεῖν οὐκ ἠδύνατο· κατεῖχεν γὰρ αὐτὸν καὶ ἡλικίας σμικρότης καὶ ἀδικίας βαρύτης. Ὅθεν νῦν ἰώμενος τῆς ἡλικίας τὴν εὐτέλειαν τῇ τῆς συνέσεως ἐπινοίᾳ προδραμὼν ἔμπροσθεν ἀνέβη ἐπὶ συκομοραίαν καὶ κρύπτεται ὑπὸ τὸ ἀμφιλαφὲς τῶν φύλλων οἰόμενος ὁρᾶν καὶ μὴ ὁρᾶσθαι, νομίζων λανθάνειν τὸν πάντα εἰδότα· ὃ δὴ καὶ ἡ αἱμορροοῦσα ὑπέστη οἰομένη κλέπτειν τὸν Ἰησοῦν τὸν ἡδέως τὰ τοιαῦτα κλεπτόμενον. Ἀλλ' ἐκείνη κἂν ἐγγὺς γενομένη τοῦ κρασπέδου ἐφήψατο, οὗτος δὲ πόρρωθεν ὢν πίστει τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐπελάβετο. Ὅθεν ἄνεισιν ἐπὶ τὸ ξύλον τὰ τοῦ Ἀδὰμ θεραπεύων κακά· ὁ μὲνγὰρ ὑπὸ τοῦ ξύλου πλανᾶται τὸν θεὸν φεύγων, ὁ δὲ ἀπὸ ξύλου σῴζεται τὸν θεὸν ἰδεῖν ἐπιθυμῶν. Ἀκούων γὰρ ὡς πολλὰ καὶ παράδοξα ἐργάζεται θαύματα, ὡς πρὸς τοῖς σώμασιν καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς ἰατρεύει, τῶν μὲν ψυχῶν τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἀφαιρούμενος, τοῖς δὲ σώμασιν ἀπάθειαν χαριζόμενος, ἐπεθύμησεν ἰδεῖν τὸν πάντα πᾶσι συγχωροῦντα λογισάμενος παρ' ἑαυτῷ·«Τίς ποτε ἆρά ἐστιν οὗτος ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὁ λεπροὺς καθαίρων, ὁ τυφλοὺς ἰώμενος, ὁ τὰ ἁμαρτήματα τοῖς αἰτοῦσι συγχωρῶν; Ποταπὸς τὸ εἶδος, ὁποῖος τὴν μορφήν; Ἆρα πάντα οἶδεν; ἆρα καὶ τῶν ἀπόντων τὰς γνώμας δοκιμάζει; ἢ τῶν συνόντων μόνον τοὺς λογισμοὺς ἐξετάζει; ἆρα ὡς θεὸς τῆς ἑκάστου καρδίας ἀνιχνεύει τὰ νοήματα; Πόθεν οὖν ταῦτα γνῶ; τίνα τούτων διδάσκαλον λάβω; τίνα; Τὴν πεῖραν, τὴν πάντων διδάσκαλον. Ἀνελθὼν ἐπὶ τὸ δένδρον κρύπτομαι ὑπὸ τὸ ἀμφιλαφὲς τῶν φύλλων. Λανθάνω καὶ μανθάνω εἰ δύναμαι σωθῆναι. Ἐὰν γνῷ μου τῆς ψυχῆς τὸ κίνημα, οἶδα ὅτι ἐξαλείφει μου τὸ τῆς ψυχῆς ἁμάρτημα· ἓν τοῦτο οὖν γνώσομαι ὅτι οἶδεν τῶν λογισμῶν τὰ κρυπτά. Ἐὰν ὑπὸ τοῦ πλήθους συνεχόμενος ἴδῃ με τὸν λανθάνοντα καὶ μὴ μόνον ἴδῃ ἀλλὰ καὶ τῆς ψυχῆς μου ἐκκαλύψῃ τὸν ἔρωτα, αἱροῦμαι πάντα ῥῖψαι καὶ ἕνα εὑρεῖν. Μιμήσασθαι Ματθαῖον θέλω· καὶ γὰρ ἐκεῖνος τελώνης ἦν ὡς καὶ ἐγώ, ἀλλὰ Ματθαῖος μὲν οὐκ αὐθαιρέτως προσέδραμεν, ἀλλὰ κληθεὶς ὑπήκουσεν. Τάχα δὲ αὐτὸν καὶ ὁρῶν καὶ ἕνα τῶν ὁδοιπόρων νομίζων τὰς χεῖρας ἐκοίλανεν καὶ βαθὺν ἐφήπλωσε κόλπον τῇ συνηθείᾳ πρὸς τὴν λῆψιν ὀχηματιζόμενος καὶ τελωνῆσαι τὸν Χριστὸν θέλων ἀντετελωνήθη παρ' αὐτοῦ οὐδὲ κατὰ σχῆμα, ἀλλ' ὅλον ἑαυτὸν ἐπιδούς. Ἅμα γὰρ ἤκουσεν· ∆εῦρο ὀπίσω μου, ὑπερέβη τὴν κλῆσιν τῇ προθυμίᾳ ὀξυτέρῳ τάχει παρατρέχων τῷ ἐφελκομένῳ. Εἰ τελώνας οὖν καλεῖ καὶ οὐ καλεῖ μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ δικαιοῖ, οὐ βλάπτει με τῶν προλαβόντων κακῶν ὁ ἑσμός· εἰ γὰρ ὁ Ἐλισσαῖος ἅλας ἐπιβαλὼν τῇ θρεψαμένῃ πηγῇ τὸ ἄγονον αὐτῆς γόνιμον εἰργάσατο, πάντως καὶ αὐτὸς τῇ χάριτι ὡς ἅλατι ἀρτύσας μου τὴν ψυχὴν καρπογονίαν ἀρετῆς 3 διεγείρει «.Ταῦτα δὲ ἐνθυμουμένου αὐτοῦ ἦλθεν ἐπὶ τὸν τόπον ὁ Ἰησοῦς· ἀναβλέψας λέγει αὐτῷ· Ζακχαῖε, σπεύσας κατάβηθι. Ἀνέβης εἰς τὸ δένδρον ὡς τελώνης, κατάβηθι ἐκ τοῦ δένδρου ὡς φιλόθεος. Κατάβα ἐκ τοῦ ξύλου ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, ἵνα ἀναβῇς διὰ τοῦ σταυροῦ πρὸς οὐρανόν. Ἀνῆλθες ἐπὶ δένδρον ἀνθρώπους κρυπτόμενος, ἀνέρχῃ διὰ τοῦ σταυροῦ ἀγγέλοις χαριζόμενος.
thought_title: Zacchaeus climbs the sycamore to test whether Jesus knows hearts
orientation: Amphilochius is imagining Zacchaeus's interior reasoning as he climbs the sycamore to see Jesus, after describing how Zacchaeus exploited shepherds and travelers.
pass_a_gloss: A shepherd living with drought and burning heat, with rain and snow and frost, having as a hut the projections of the rocks, as food cheese and milk, as a garment the unworked hide of the sheep, but this rustic man, the poor man, the man conversing with mountains, used to fall in with Zacchaeus, being tithed of his flocks, being robbed lawfully, being destroyed without a sword. For the man struck by iron and receiving an easy wound departs, having escaped by insensibility the harshness of the suffering, but the man shot by involuntary poverty has pain as death and has died; not being spent once, but he dies always little by little. And that I may speak briefly, just as to soldiers the hard-to-capture forts and to pilots the underwater rocks and to those at war the suspected ambushes, so to merchants and travelers, to cowherds and shepherds Zacchaeus was to be fled. But this man, so raging about the irrational collection of money, seeking to see Jesus was not able; for both smallness of stature and heaviness of injustice held him. Therefore now healing the cheapness of his stature by the device of his understanding, having run ahead, he went up onto a sycamore and hides himself under the thick foliage of the leaves, thinking to see and not to be seen, supposing to escape the notice of the one who knows all things; which very thing also the woman with the flow of blood underwent, thinking to steal Jesus, who is gladly stolen in such ways. But she, even having come near, touched the hem, but this man, being far off, took hold of Christ by faith. Therefore he goes up onto the tree, healing the evils of Adam; for the one is led astray by the tree, fleeing God, but the other is saved from the tree, desiring to see God. For hearing that he works many and paradoxical wonders, that in addition to bodies he also heals souls, taking away the sins of souls, and granting to bodies freedom from suffering, he desired to see the one forgiving all things to all, reasoning within himself: "Who ever then is this Jesus, the one cleansing lepers, the one healing the blind, the one forgiving sins to those who ask? Of what sort in appearance, of what kind in form? Does he know all things? Does he also test the minds of those who are absent? Or does he examine only the thoughts of those who are present? Does he as God track the thoughts of each person's heart? From where then shall I know these things? What teacher of these things shall I take? What teacher? Experience, the teacher of all things. Having gone up onto the tree I hide myself under the thick foliage of the leaves. I escape notice and I learn whether I am able to be saved. If he knows the movement of my soul, I know that he wipes out the sin of my soul; this one thing therefore I shall know, that he knows the hidden things of thoughts. If, pressed by the crowd, he sees me who am hiding and not only sees but also uncovers the love of my soul, I choose to cast away all things and to find the one. I wish to imitate Matthew; for that man also was a tax collector as I also am, but Matthew did not run up of his own accord, but having been called he obeyed. Perhaps also seeing him and thinking him one of the travelers, he hollowed his hands and spread wide a deep bosom, being carried along by habit toward the taking, and wishing to tax Christ he was taxed in return by him, not even in appearance, but giving over his whole self. For at once he heard: Come after me, he surpassed the call by eagerness, running past with swifter speed the one drawing him along. If therefore he calls tax collectors and not only calls but also justifies, the swarm of my previous evils does not harm me; for if Elisha, having cast salt into the spring that nourished him, made its barrenness fruitful, surely he also, having seasoned my soul with grace as with salt, stirs up fruit-bearing of virtue." And while he was pondering these things, Jesus came to the place; looking up he says to him: Zacchaeus, having hurried come down. You went up into the tree as a tax collector, come down from the tree as a lover of God. Come down from the tree onto the earth, so that you may go up through the cross to heaven. You went up onto a tree hiding from men, you go up through the cross giving joy to angels.

lemmas.gloss: woman with a flow of blood

choices.why: Keeps the passive force of the shepherd as victim and the specific tenth-tax sense of δεκατεύω, matching the homily's picture of Zacchaeus as exploiter.
Preserves the oxymoron of legalized robbery that the preacher is building against tax collectors.
Keeps the violent verb ἀναιρέω and the explicit absence of a weapon, showing the hidden lethality of Zacchaeus's extortion.
rejected: put to death without a sword

choices.english: by the device of his understanding
choices.why: ἐπίνοια is a contrivance or stratagem, and σύνεσις is practical understanding; together they capture Zacchaeus's clever plan to overcome his stature.
rejected: by the thought of his intelligence

choices.why: Keeps the typological force of Zacchaeus's tree-climbing as a remedy for Adam's fall at the tree, with θεραπεύω as healing.

choices.english: he was taxed in return by him
choices.why: The coined verb ἀντιτελωνέω is a deliberate wordplay on τελώνης; rendering it as 'taxed in return' preserves the pun and the reversal.
rejected: was made a tax collector by him

pass_b_english: A shepherd lived with drought and burning heat, with rain and snow and frost. His shelter was the ledges of the rocks, his food cheese and milk, his clothing the unworked skins of his sheep. Yet this rustic, this poor man, this companion of the mountains, fell into Zacchaeus's hands, being tithed of his flocks, being robbed lawfully, being destroyed without a sword. For a man struck by iron receives a wound that flows easily and departs, escaping the harshness of his suffering through numbness. But a man unwillingly shot by poverty's arrow has pain as his death, and he has died, not consumed all at once, but dying always, little by little. And to put it briefly: as fortresses hard to capture are dreaded by soldiers, and underwater rocks by pilots, and hidden ambushes by those at war, so Zacchaeus was to be fled by merchants and travelers, by cowherds and shepherds.

But this man, so maddened over the irrational collection of money, was seeking to see Jesus and could not. For both the smallness of his stature and the heaviness of his injustice held him back. So now, healing the lowliness of his stature by the device of his understanding, he ran ahead and climbed up into a sycamore, and he hides himself under the dense cover of the leaves, thinking he sees and is not seen, supposing he can escape the notice of the one who knows all things. This is exactly what the woman with the flow of blood also ventured, thinking she could steal from Jesus, the one who gladly lets such things be stolen from him. But she at least came near and touched the hem of his garment; this man, being far off, took hold of Christ by faith. So he goes up onto the tree, healing the evils of Adam. For Adam was led astray by the tree while fleeing God, but this man is saved from the tree while longing to see God.

For hearing that Jesus works many astonishing wonders, that he heals souls as well as bodies, taking away the sins of souls and granting freedom from suffering to bodies, Zacchaeus longed to see the one who pardons all things to all people. He reasoned within himself:

"Who then is this Jesus, who cleanses lepers, who heals the blind, who forgives sins to those who ask? What is his appearance, what is his form? Does he know all things? Does he test the minds even of those who are absent? Or does he examine only the thoughts of those who are present? Does he, as God, trace out the thoughts of each person's heart? How then can I learn these things? What teacher shall I take for them? What teacher? Experience, the teacher of all things. I have climbed the tree and hide myself under the dense cover of the leaves. I escape notice and I learn whether I can be saved. If he knows the movement of my soul, I know that he wipes away the sin of my soul. This one thing then I will learn: that he knows the hidden things of my thoughts. If, pressed by the crowd, he sees me hiding, and not only sees me but also uncovers the longing of my soul, I choose to throw away everything and find the one. I want to imitate Matthew. For he too was a tax collector, as I am. But Matthew did not run to him of his own accord; rather, he was called and obeyed. Perhaps, seeing him and thinking him one of the travelers, he hollowed his hands and spread wide his deep pocket, carried along by habit toward the taking, and wanting to collect taxes from Christ, he was collected from in return by him, not in appearance only, but giving his whole self over. For as soon as he heard, 'Come, follow me,' he outran the call with his eagerness, outrunning with swifter speed the one who drew him. If then he calls tax collectors, and not only calls them but also makes them righteous, the swarm of my previous evils does not harm me. For if Elisha threw salt into the nourishing spring and made its barrenness fruitful, surely this man also, seasoning my soul with grace as with salt, stirs up in me the fruit-bearing of virtue."

While he was pondering these things, Jesus came to the place. Looking up, he says to him: "Zacchaeus, hurry and come down. You climbed the tree as a tax collector; come down from the tree as a lover of God. Come down from the tree to the earth, so that through the cross you may go up to heaven. You went up a tree hiding from human beings; you are going up through the cross, granting a gift to angels."

problems.quote: the cheapness of his stature
problems.why: εὐτέλειαν means 'smallness, lowliness,' not 'cheapness' (which implies worthlessness)
problems.fix: the lowliness of his stature

problems.quote: he surpassed the call with his eagerness, running past with a speed swifter than the one drawing him
problems.source_quote: ὑπερέβη τὴν κλῆσιν τῇ προθυμίᾳ ὀξυτέρῳ τάχει παρατρέχων τῷ ἐφελκομένῳ
problems.why: τῷ ἐφελκομένῳ is dative: 'than the one drawing him'—but παρατρέχων takes genitive, so this is 'running past the one drawing him with swifter speed'
problems.fix: he outran the call with his eagerness, passing by the one who drew him with a swifter speed

problems.quote: the spring that nourished him
problems.why: θρεψαμένῃ is middle: 'that had nourished' (the city/people), not 'that nourished him'—Elisha threw salt into the spring that had nourished
problems.fix: the spring that had nourished

problems.quote: Perhaps when he saw him and thought he was one of the travelers, he hollowed his hands
problems.source_quote: Τάχα δὲ αὐτὸν καὶ ὁρῶν καὶ ἕνα τῶν ὁδοιπόρων νομίζων τὰς χεῖρας ἐκοίλανεν
problems.why: This is still Zacchaeus's interior monologue about his own plan; 'when he saw him' wrongly shifts subject and tense to a past narrative event.
problems.fix: Perhaps, seeing him and thinking him one of the travelers, I will hollow my hands
problems.ruling: Greek 'Τάχα δὲ αὐτὸν καὶ ὁρῶν' is Zacchaeus's imagined future self; 'when he saw him' shifts to past narrative, breaking monologue.

problems.quote: Perhaps when he saw him and thought he was one of the travelers, he hollowed his hands and spread wide his deep pocket, carried along by habit toward the taking, and wanting to tax Christ, he was taxed in return by him
problems.source_quote: Τάχα δὲ αὐτὸν καὶ ὁρῶν καὶ ἕνα τῶν ὁδοιπόρων νομίζων τὰς χεῖρας ἐκοίλανεν καὶ βαθὺν ἐφήπλωσε κόλπον τῇ συνηθείᾳ πρὸς τὴν λῆψιν ὠχηματιζόμενος καὶ τελωνῆσαι τὸν Χριστὸν θέλων ἀντετελώνηται παρ' αὐτοῦ
problems.why: Entire clause is Zacchaeus's imagined first-person plan; English renders it as third-person past narrative, confusing whose words these are.
problems.fix: Perhaps, seeing him and thinking him one of the travelers, I will hollow my hands and spread wide my deep pocket, carried along by habit toward the taking, and wanting to tax Christ, I will be taxed in return by him
problems.ruling: Greek first-person subjunctive plan ('ἐκοίλανεν' as 'I will hollow') rendered as third-person past, losing speaker identity throughout.

problems.quote: shot with the arrow of involuntary poverty
problems.why: ἀκουσίῳ goes with τετοξευμένος (unwillingly/unwittingly shot), not 'involuntary poverty'
problems.fix: unwillingly shot by poverty's arrow
problems.ruling: ἀκουσίῳ πενίᾳ: 'unwitting poverty' shot him; not 'arrow of involuntary poverty'—misread syntax.

edits.old: he surpassed the call with his eagerness, running past with a speed swifter than the one drawing him
edits.new: he outran the call with his eagerness, passing by the one who drew him with a swifter speed

edits.old: Perhaps when he saw him and thought he was one of the travelers, he hollowed his hands and spread wide his deep pocket, carried along by habit toward the taking, and wanting to tax Christ, he was taxed in return by him
edits.new: Perhaps, seeing him and thinking him one of the travelers, I will hollow my hands and spread wide my deep pocket, carried along by habit toward the taking, and wanting to tax Christ, I will be taxed in return by him

edits.old: shot with the arrow of involuntary poverty

fixed: The speaker problem is resolved by the same edit that fixes the mistranslation of the Matthew passage.
The 'spring that nourished him' edit removes the incorrect 'him' and uses the middle sense 'had nourished'.

problems.quote: giving over his whole self
problems.why: ἐπιδούς means 'giving himself over/up' (to Christ), but 'his' wrongly makes it Christ giving himself; Zacchaeus speaks of himself giving himself.
problems.fix: giving my whole self over

problems.quote: passing by the one who drew him with a swifter speed
problems.why: παρατρέχων τῷ ἐφελκομένῳ means 'outrunning the one who drew him'—Matthew runs ahead of Jesus, not 'passing by'.
problems.fix: outrunning with swifter speed the one who drew him

problems.quote: the spring that had nourished
problems.why: θρεψαμένῃ is middle 'that had nourished itself' or passive 'that was nourished'—the spring was self-nourishing/barren, not nourishing others.
problems.fix: the self-nourishing spring

problems.quote: This is exactly what the woman with the flow of blood also endured
problems.source_quote: ἃ δὴ καὶ ἡ αἱμορροοῦσα ὑπέστη
problems.why: ὑπέστη means 'undertook' or 'ventured', not 'endured'; she attempted the same thing.
problems.fix: This is exactly what the woman with the flow of blood also ventured
problems.ruling: ὑπέστη means 'undertook/ventured', not 'endured'; the woman attempted the same hiding, not suffered it.

problems.quote: being tithed of his flocks, being robbed lawfully
problems.why: ἐννόμως means 'unlawfully'/'illegally', not 'lawfully'—the point is Zacchaeus's robbery was legalized injustice, not truly lawful.
problems.fix: being tithed of his flocks, being robbed illegally
problems.ruling: ἐννόμως means 'lawfully/legally'; the irony is legal robbery. But 'lawfully' misses the injustice nuance—minor, not major.

problems.quote: giving over his whole self
problems.why: The shift to 'his' makes it seem like Jesus is the subject, confusing Zacchaeus's interior monologue about his own intended action.
problems.fix: giving my whole self over
problems.ruling: ὅλον ἑαυτὸν ἐπιδούς: Zacchaeus says 'I give over my whole self'; 'his' wrongly shifts subject to Jesus, misleading readers.

edits.old: being tithed of his flocks, being robbed lawfully
edits.new: being tithed of his flocks, being robbed illegally

edits.old: This is exactly what the woman with the flow of blood also endured
edits.new: This is exactly what the woman with the flow of blood also ventured

edits.old: but giving over his whole self
edits.new: but giving my whole self over

edits.old: passing by the one who drew him with a swifter speed
edits.new: outrunning with swifter speed the one who drew him

fixed: The speaker issue for 'giving over his whole self' is resolved by the edit changing 'his' to 'my', which restores Zacchaeus as the subject of his own interior monologue.

problems.quote: self-nourishing spring
problems.why: θρεψαμένῃ means 'nourishing' (active), not 'self-nourishing'; the spring nourishes others.
problems.fix: the nourishing spring

problems.quote: wanting to tax Christ, I will be taxed in return by him
problems.source_quote: τελωνῆσαι τὸν Χριστὸν θέλων ἀντετελωνήθη παρ' αὐτοῦ
problems.why: τελωνέω means to collect taxes, but here Zacchaeus plans to 'tax' Christ (collect from him) and instead is 'taxed in return'—yet ἀντετελωνήθη suggests reciprocal action, better as 'collect in return'.
problems.fix: wanting to collect taxes from Christ, I was collected from in return by him

problems.quote: not in appearance only, but giving my whole self over
problems.source_quote: οὐδὲ κατὰ σχῆμα, ἀλλ' ὅλον ἑαυτὸν ἐπιδούς
problems.why: The subject shifts to Matthew here, not Zacchaeus; Matthew gave his whole self, not Zacchaeus planning to.
problems.fix: not in appearance only, but giving his whole self over

problems.quote: the one who forgives everything to everyone
problems.why: πάντα πᾶσι means 'all things to all people', but συγχωροῦντα is 'forgiving' or 'pardoning'—the sense is 'the one who pardons all things to all people'.
problems.fix: the one who pardons all things to all people

problems.quote: I will climb the tree and hide myself under the dense cover of the leaves. I escape notice and I learn
problems.source_quote: Ἀνελθὼν ἐπὶ τὸ δένδρον κρύπτομαι... Λανθάνω καὶ μανθάνω
problems.why: Zacchaeus says 'I have climbed' (aorist participle) and 'I escape notice and learn' (present), not future 'I will climb'.
problems.fix: I have climbed the tree and hide myself under the dense cover of the leaves. I escape notice and I learn
problems.ruling: Ἀνελθὼν is aorist participle 'having climbed', not future; λανθάνω/μανθάνω are present indicatives 'I escape notice and learn', not future.

problems.quote: I will hollow my hands and spread wide my deep pocket
problems.source_quote: τὰς χεῖρας ἐκοίλανεν καὶ βαθὺν ἐφήπλωσε κόλπον
problems.why: Verbs are 3rd person ('he hollowed'), describing Matthew, not 1st person Zacchaeus.
problems.fix: he hollowed his hands and spread wide his deep pocket
problems.ruling: ἐκοίλανεν and ἐφήπλωσε are 3rd person aorist indicatives describing Matthew's action, not Zacchaeus's 1st person intention.

problems.quote: surely this man also, seasoning my soul with grace as with salt, will stir up in me the fruit-bearing of virtue
problems.source_quote: πάντως καὶ αὐτὸς τῇ χάριτι ὡς ἅλατι ἀρτύσας μου τὴν ψυχὴν καρπογονίαν ἀρετῆς διεγείρει
problems.why: ἀρτύσας and διεγείρει are 3rd person ('seasoning...he stirs up'), not 'seasoning...will stir up'.
problems.fix: surely this man also, seasoning my soul with grace as with salt, stirs up in me the fruit-bearing of virtue
problems.ruling: ἀρτύσας is aorist participle 'having seasoned', διεγείρει is present indicative 'he stirs up', not future 'will stir up'.

problems.quote: giving joy to angels
problems.why: χαριζόμενος means 'granting' or 'bestowing', not 'giving joy'; Zacchaeus grants angels something (a saved soul to rejoice over).
problems.fix: granting a gift to angels
problems.ruling: χαριζόμενος means 'granting/bestowing,' not 'giving joy'; Zacchaeus bestows something upon angels, not joy per se.

problems.quote: being tithed of his flocks, being robbed illegally
problems.why: ἐννόμως means 'lawfully' or 'legally', not 'illegally'—the point is Zacchaeus robs legally (through taxes), which is worse.
problems.fix: being tithed of his flocks, being robbed lawfully
problems.ruling: ἐννόμως means 'lawfully/legally,' not 'illegally'; the irony is Zacchaeus robs legally via tithing, reversing the expected meaning.
